p: Prototype: course PoE IP camera + 48 V PoE injector + isolated gigabit switch + Radxa ROCK 4C+ running my FFmpeg/Python event recorder, viewed and stored on a MacBook.
Source code (GitHub): https://github.com/OrsonJyu/Lab-Studies-in-Systems-Design · camera module: project-camera/ · Slides: camera-module section in our team Figma deck

ul.li: Sensor evaluated: PoE IP camera (GK7205V200, 2560×1440 H.264 at 20 fps + 800×448 substream, ONVIF), powered over the network cable.
Target controller: Radxa ROCK 4C+ (RK3399, Debian 12) instead of ESP32-C3, because the camera delivers compressed video over Ethernet (reasons in section 4.1).

Main result: the recorder keeps the 4–6 s before each movement, and in the final on-site test it recorded only when the tracked (toy) gecko moved: 3 of 3 clips correct, 0 clips of a hand moving in the enclosure.
Not yet shown: a real gecko, night (IR) recording and multi-day running. These are listed in section 8.

p: I evaluated whether a PoE IP camera, driven by a small Linux board, can produce useful gecko video automatically: start recording when the gecko moves, keep the moment before it moved, ignore people and lighting changes, and hand each clip over with a verifiable record.

tr.td: Sensor
PoE IP camera from the course demonstration module (GK7205V200 SoC, 2.8 mm lens, 940 nm IR LEDs)
Main stream 2560×1440 H.264, 20 fps, keyframe every 2 s; substream 800×448; RTSP video; ONVIF for device control (clock). No microphone.
Power for the sensor
48 V PoE injector with its own mains cord
Puts 48 V on the same Cat5e cable that carries the video (no separate camera power cable).
Network
8-port gigabit switch with its own power adapter
Isolated wired network: camera, ROCK and Mac only; no internet on this network.
Target controller
Radxa ROCK 4C+ (RK3399, 6 cores), Debian 12, Python 3.11, FFmpeg 5.1
Receives both streams, keeps the RAM ring buffer, runs detection and tracking, serves the live web page.
Host
MacBook + USB-C dock (Ethernet)
Web view, clip storage (recordings/), and USB-C power for the ROCK 4C+.

h2: 2. Why this sensor, and how it fits Project 2 (Video Recording Module)
p: Team 02 is assigned Project 2: Video Recording Module of the Final Project (an IoT system that helps primary and secondary students observe and care for a leopard gecko). Video is the only sensor in our system that gives evidence a student can replay: where the gecko went, when it was active, and what happened before. Leopard geckos are mostly active at dusk and night, so the camera’s 940 nm IR illumination matters for later work.
Following step 2 of the course’s Generic Workflow, I defined the data input, processing logic and output:

tr.td: Main stream (2560×1440) for the record; substream (800×448) for analysis; camera clock via ONVIF

Keep the last 60 s in RAM. Find changes inside the area we drew; ignore whole-picture changes; locate and lock on the gecko; start an event when the locked gecko really moves for 0.5 s; end it after 5 s of stillness.
One MP4 clip per event (from ~4 s before the first movement) + JSON record (times, segments, SHA-256), moved to the host; live web page with the gecko box, detection area and a clickable timeline.

ul.li: The gecko walks out of its hide → a clip that also shows the seconds before it moved.
A student’s hand or a teacher reaching in, people walking past, lights switched on → no clip.
Other teams (Hide, feeders, thermal) need clips with trustworthy times → the camera clock is set from the ROCK at every start, and every clip has a JSON record.

p.em: The same wiring as a picture (devices drawn with Figma AI; cables and ports drawn by me from the real setup).
Two streams, two FFmpeg processes, one clip per event.

ul.li: FFmpeg #1 (recorder): copies the main stream, without re-encoding, into 2 s MPEG-TS segments in a 60 s RAM ring (/dev/shm).
FFmpeg #2 (detector): scales the substream to 160×90 at 10 fps and outputs, per frame, a grey-change mask (|ΔY| > 15), a colour-change mask (|ΔU|+|ΔV| > 24) and the Y, U, V planes.
Python (standard library only): detection-area rules, gecko tracker, event logic, clip assembly, live web page (MJPEG + JSON API).
Mac side: clips are copied, SHA-256-checked, and only then deleted on the ROCK; the camera clock is set over ONVIF at every start.

p: Requirements: ROCK 4C+ with Debian 12, Python ≥ 3.9 and FFmpeg; a macOS or Linux host with Python 3 and ssh; the camera, injector and switch wired as in 4.2, with static addresses on the isolated network.

ol.li: git clone https://github.com/OrsonJyu/Lab-Studies-in-Systems-Design.git then git checkout code/demo-installer (the one-command installer is in pull request #12 and not yet merged into main; the recorder itself is already on main)
python3 project-camera/demo/demo.py setup — checks the network, logs in to the ROCK (password typed by the user), checks Python/FFmpeg, deploys the code with SHA-256 checks and runs the tests.

python3 project-camera/demo/demo.py status / stop — state, clip count; stop also moves the last clips to the host.
Tests only: python3 -m unittest discover -s project-camera/src/recorder

p: Full step-by-step guide (Chinese, with an English section): project-camera/demo/README.md (branch code/demo-installer).

I built the module in small steps. Each step answered one question; when a test showed a problem, the next step fixed it. All tests were on the real camera and ROCK; a green toy lizard stood in for the gecko. Images marked “replay” were produced by feeding a recorded clip back through the same detector and tracker code, so that the boxes could be drawn on every frame.

p.em: [PHOTOS OF THE REAL SETUP — to be added]

h3: 5.2 Step 1 (30 Oct) — Can the ROCK receive and save the camera stream?

tr.td: First check of the whole chain: PoE camera → switch → ROCK, recording with FFmpeg over RTSP.
FFmpeg on the ROCK records 60 s of the main stream with stream copy; the file is fully decoded and copied to the Mac with a SHA-256 check.

Home: 1,201 frames in 60 s (20.4 fps, 2.1 Mbit/s, 0 dropped, 0 duplicated). School: 60.001 s, 1,200 frames, full decode with no errors, copy hash matched. FFmpeg warned about unset/non-monotonic timestamps from the camera, so clip timing must not rely on camera timestamps.

p.em: A frame from the first 60 s recording (IR lights on).

h3: 5.3 Step 2 (5 Nov, home) — How late is the video, and are the clocks right?

tr.td: If recording starts only after motion is seen, how much is lost? The camera’s on-screen clock was also wrong.
Filmed a millisecond clock on the Mac screen and compared it with the ROCK’s receive time. Set the ROCK clock from the Mac, and the camera clock from the ROCK over ONVIF.

Camera → ROCK delay 0.19–0.29 s (median 0.23 s). Starting FFmpeg after a trigger loses ≈0.4 s plus ≈2 s before the first output, so the start of a movement would be lost → a ring buffer is required. Camera clock was ≈28 days slow; after setting it, 0.3 s off. It resets on power loss, so it is now set automatically at every start.

p.em: Latency test: the camera films the Mac clock (left, middle); first frame received on the ROCK at school (right).

h3: 5.4 Step 3 — Never miss the start: RAM ring buffer

tr.td: Keep the seconds before a movement without recording everything to storage.
FFmpeg #1 never stops and writes 2 s segments into a 60 s RAM ring. When an event closes, the segments from ≥4 s before the first motion to 5 s after the last motion are joined into one MP4.

Manual triggers kept 5.0–5.6 s before the trigger; hand tests kept 3.7–4.65 s before the hand appeared, with 0.45–0.65 s detection delay. In the clip below the gecko was pulled at 5.1 s, and the pre-roll shows it still before that.

p.em: A real clip with its timeline: cyan = pre-roll already in RAM, lime = gecko moving, grey = 5 s still, then close (download)
The same clip as saved by the recorder (2560×1440, 21 s) (download)

h3: 5.5 Step 4 — Stage 1: any changed pixel starts a recording

tr.td: Can simple frame differencing tell when something moved?
motion_filter(): FFmpeg subtracts each 160×90 frame from the previous one and keeps pixels whose brightness changed by more than the threshold; a second mask does the same for colour.
It reacts quickly, but in a real classroom it cannot tell what moved: 86 recordings in 2.5 h at school, mostly people, hands, lights and auto-exposure.

p.em: Replay: camera frame and the change mask the rule sees, for a moving lizard (top) and for a hand only (bottom).

h3: 5.6 Step 5 — Stage 2: detection area and environment rules

tr.td: Ignore changes outside the enclosure and whole-picture changes.

A polygon drawn on the web page becomes a bit mask (one AND per frame); ≥30 % of the whole picture changing counts as a lighting/scene change and is ignored for 2 s; motion must last 0.5 s. Threshold lowered from 25 to 15 so a moving lizard is caught.

No triggers from activity outside the area in ≈2 min; one whole-picture change of 31.4 % (cause not visible) was classed as a scene change and ignored — only just above the 30 % limit; 201 still frames without a false trigger; ≈0.25 ms of analysis per frame. Problem left: a hand inside the area still records.

p.em: Replay: blue = detection area, red = motion found inside it.

h3: 5.7 Step 6 — Where is the gecko? Background model and tracker

tr.td: To ignore hands, the system first has to know where the gecko is.

Tracker: median background from still frames; foreground = grey difference > 30 or colour difference > 24; 8-connected blobs inside the area; lock on a blob that moves; follow it by overlap or appearance; absorb the “ghost” it leaves in the background.

With brightness only, the box covered just the tail (lizard Y ≈ 157 vs desk 156–186). Adding colour (U 58 vs 102–115, V 81 vs 137–145): the box covered the whole lizard in 5 of 6 sampled frames, it stayed locked while still for 55 s, and reported “lost” correctly when the lizard was removed. Tracking costs ≈8 ms per frame (63 ms before optimising), ≈13 % CPU.

p.em: Why colour: in Y the lizard is nearly the desk’s grey; in U and V it stands out.
Replay frames: the box while moving and resting.
Replay: green box follows the gecko; the chip shows the tracker state (download)

h3: 5.8 Step 7 — Stage 3: record only when the gecko itself moves

tr.td: With the gecko locked, a hand moving in the area still started recordings.

Recording is triggered by the tracked gecko moving (area rules are only logged). “Moving” means the whole box shifts ≥2 px within 1 s with both opposite edges moving the same way; the blob followed must overlap the last box or look like the gecko and stay within 1/1.6–1.6× of its usual size; movement must last 0.5 s.
Pixel flicker from exposure/shadow counted as movement → require real travel + 0.5 s
Hand shadow merged with the gecko and pulled the box → whole-box edge shift, overlap/appearance check, size band
Hand in the area for 8 s: 87 frames fired the area rule, none recorded; 3 gecko clips kept

p.em: Replay: red = area rule fires, green = gecko box; only the gecko moving records.
Replay: a hand waves while the gecko rests; the chips show what each trigger would do (download)

h2: 7. Reflection: is it suitable for our design solution?
p: Yes, for the daytime video recording function. The ring buffer solved the problem that mattered most for evidence (the start of a movement is never lost), and moving the trigger from “any change” to “the gecko moved” took false recordings from tens per hour to none in the final test. The board copes easily: the heavy per-pixel work stays inside FFmpeg and the Python analysis runs on 160×90 frames.

What I learned: each rule fixed one failure but exposed the next one (exposure flicker, then the hand’s shadow). Testing on site, replaying the recorded clips through the same code and writing each result down was what made the fixes possible.

ul.li: All tests used a toy lizard in daylight; a real gecko is smaller, slower and often still for long periods, and the IR night mode is untested.
Longest run so far is ≈2.5 h. The ROCK stopped suddenly twice on 5 Nov under light load. It is powered from the Mac’s USB-C port, which is the first suspect (not confirmed).
The camera loses its clock when power is cut; this is handled by setting it at every start.
When the gecko is pulled fast, the box can stay ≈2 s on the spot it left.
Not yet connected to Node-RED or the other teams’ data; the module is not yet mounted on the enclosure.

p: Improvements: give the ROCK its own 5 V / 3 A supply and run for 24 h; test at night with IR and the real gecko; publish events (time, position, clip link) to Node-RED; agree camera position and field of view with the Enclosure and Hide teams.

p: This page and the work on it are mine (ZHU Kecheng). I set up and wired the camera, PoE injector, switch and ROCK 4C+, ran every test at home and at school, decided each design change from the test results, drew the detection areas and judged each recorded clip. The code, test replays and documentation were developed with AI assistance (Claude Code) under my direction, and are versioned in our GitHub repository. The camera, injector and course demonstration-module information come from the course page linked in section 3. Teammates’ studies (e.g. the thermal array) are on their own pages.
